hypothesis: ggml's f32 CONCAT (the Gated DeltaNet conv_input concat in each of qwen35's 18 linear-attention layers) splits work by dst dim 2 only, so a one-sequence ubatch copies on one of six threads while five wait. Splitting it by rows across all threads removes most of that copy's wall time; warm requests get up to about 5 % faster, with bit-identical answers.

conclusion: NO-CHANGE on Lambda. Answers are bit-identical: 1126/1126 rows-arm answers against P1's reference, the same for ctl, and 1270/1270 rows answers against ctl in the same run. The warm forward did not get faster. On CPU part 0xd40 every one of 35 (round, request, leg) cells fell within the control's own spread, the median cell delta was +0.70 %, and the environment-level 95 % intervals range from -1.7 % to +3.9 % depending on request, with both signs present. Parts 0xd4f and 0xd0c also show both signs and no consistent gain. Offline on an arm64 host (part 0xd40, kernel 6.1, CPUs pinned, NOT LAMBDA) the same patch was 2-6 % faster in 4 interleaved rounds. The Lambda/offline difference is in the effect, not in the cost: a diagnostic function on Lambda timed the concat on thread 0 at the same calls per request and the same milliseconds as offline on 0xd40 (ticket-route-1q 16.8 vs 16.8 ms, agent-action-guard-2q 52.5 vs 51.8 ms), about 2.6-6.9 % of engine time. P3's 5.3-5.6 % Lambda share therefore matches the concat's real wall share. The 1.2 % offline perf figure was whole-run CPU share including model load, and the steady-state CPU share there was 2.65 %. The sampler's thread delivery was checked on Lambda (main-thread share 15.8 % vs fair 16.7 %) and does not explain the gap. Why removing the single-threaded wait does not shorten a Lambda forward is not established; one untested candidate is that idle OpenMP workers spinning at the barrier contend with the copying thread under Lambda's CPU allocation. No deployment change recommended.
